label: A pigmented lesion in question
q: Does this need to come off?
lead: This presentation is asymmetric in its costs. Excising a benign nevus costs a scar; missing a melanoma costs a life. Set your threshold accordingly, and remember that the ABCDE rule does not apply to nodular melanoma — which is why change, elevation and bleeding matter as much as the ABCDE letters.

stop.l: A new or changing nodule, firm, elevated and growing over weeks
stop.a: Nodular or amelanotic melanoma until excluded. ABCDE does not apply here — nodular melanoma is symmetric, uniform and small when it is already deep. Excise, do not monitor.

stop.l: A pigmented band in a single nail with proximal nail fold pigmentation
stop.a: Hutchinson sign. Subungual melanoma. Nail matrix biopsy — not a course of antifungal.

stop.l: An ulcerated or bleeding pigmented lesion
stop.a: Ulceration is an adverse prognostic feature and upstages a melanoma. Excise urgently for definitive histology.

stop.l: An acral pigmented lesion with irregular parallel ridge pigmentation on dermoscopy
stop.a: Acral lentiginous melanoma. This subtype is the commonest melanoma in darker skin types and is diagnosed late because it is dismissed as a bruise or a callus.

stop.l: Any pigmented lesion the patient says has changed, even if it looks benign
stop.a: Reported change is a stronger predictor than any static feature. Take a history of change seriously and either excise or arrange short-interval digital dermoscopic follow-up.

stop.l: A new nodule, focal color change or ulceration arising inside a large congenital nevus
stop.a: Melanoma in a congenital melanocytic nevus. It arises in the dermal or subcutaneous nevomelanocytes and is already deep when it first becomes visible, so the prognosis is poor. Excise the nodule now and refer - do not photograph and review.

dx.look: A small, well-defined, firm, steel-blue to blue-black papule or nodule, present for years and stable, most often on the dorsal hands and feet, scalp or sacrum; the blue color is the Tyndall effect of deep dermal melanin.
fr: Uniform steel-blue to blue-black color
Small (usually under 1 cm), firm, dome-shaped
Stable for years
Dorsa of hands and feet, scalp, sacrum
Well-defined and symmetric
ag: Recent change, growth or asymmetry
Multiple colors or an atypical network
Larger than 1 cm, or cellular or plaque-type (needs excision)
dx.cf: A stable, symmetric, uniformly blue lesion is typically benign; excise any new, changing, large or cellular blue nodule to exclude blue-nevus-like melanoma.
dx.dsc: A homogeneous steel-blue structureless pattern without network, dots or globules - the classic hallmark of a common blue nevus.
dx.hp: Dendritic and spindled, heavily pigmented melanocytes among sclerotic dermal collagen; the common type is bland, while cellular blue nevi are more crowded and enter the melanoma differential.
dx.assoc: Usually solitary and benign; multiple or agminated blue nevi and the epithelioid variant can occur in the Carney complex - assess for that in the right context.
dx.mgmt: Reassurance for a stable, typical lesion; excise new, enlarging, large (over 1 cm) or cellular lesions to exclude melanoma histologically.
dx.pat: Dorsal hands and feet, scalp, sacrum

dx.look: A rapidly appearing, dome-shaped, pink (or pigmented) smooth papule, usually in a child or young adult and most often on the face or legs; benign, but histologically it overlaps with melanoma, so it is managed cautiously.
fr: Child or young adult
Rapid initial growth then stability
Pink, smooth, dome-shaped papule (or a pigmented starburst)
Solitary and small (usually under 1 cm)
Symmetric
ag: Older adult
Ongoing growth, ulceration or asymmetry
Larger than 1 cm - increasingly worrisome
dx.cf: A starburst pattern on dermoscopy supports a Spitz nevus, but histology remains the gold standard; excision is generally advised for atypical, larger or adult-onset lesions given the melanoma overlap.
dx.dsc: A symmetric starburst pattern - regularly distributed peripheral streaks and pseudopods around a central hyperpigmented zone; a pink Spitz shows dotted vessels.
dx.hp: A symmetric, well-circumscribed proliferation of large spindled and epithelioid melanocytes with Kamino bodies and maturation with depth; separating atypical Spitz from spitzoid melanoma can be difficult.
dx.assoc: Benign but a histologic mimic of melanoma; atypical Spitz tumors are managed as intermediate lesions, and adult-onset spitzoid lesions warrant a low threshold for complete excision.
dx.mgmt: Complete excision is generally advised, particularly for atypical, larger or adult lesions; small classic pediatric lesions may be observed by some specialists.
dx.pat: Face and legs of a child

dx.look: Symmetric, uniformly pigmented, regular sharp border, under 6 mm, stable for years. Junctional lesions are flat and brown; compound are papular; dermal are dome-shaped, skin-colored to tan, often with telangiectasia and hairs.
fr: Symmetric with a regular border
One uniform color
Under 6 mm
Stable over years
Resembles the patient's other nevi — no ugly duckling
ag: Any reported change in size, shape or color
Multiple colors including blue-gray, white or red
Over 6 mm with an irregular notched border
Stands out from all the patient's other lesions
dx.cf: Clinical, supported by dermoscopy. Photograph and review if there is any doubt rather than excising every one.
dx.dsc: A symmetric benign pattern - uniform reticular network, globular or homogeneous - with no melanoma-specific structures.
dx.hp: Nested melanocytes at the junction, dermis or both (junctional, intradermal or compound), with maturation and dispersion at the base.
dx.assoc: Track lesions against the patient signature nevus pattern; the ugly-duckling lesion that deviates from the rest warrants scrutiny.
dx.mgmt: No treatment for typical nevi; excise only if changing, symptomatic, or dermoscopically atypical.
dx.pat: Anywhere, favoring sun-exposed trunk and limbs

dx.look: Larger than a common nevus, often over 6 mm, with a macular component extending beyond a papular center giving a fried-egg appearance. Irregular but not sharply notched border, variegated tan-brown, sometimes pink. Trunk mainly.
fr: Macular shoulder extending beyond a central papule
Variegated tan and brown
Multiple similar lesions, often with a family history
ag: Blue-white veil, regression structures or a notched border
Solitary and clearly different from all the others
Rapid change
dx.cf: Dermoscopy, with digital monitoring in patients who have many. Excise the ones that stand out, not all of them. More than 5 dysplastic nevi is itself a melanoma risk factor.
dx.dsc: An atypical network with asymmetry of color and structure and irregular peripheral pigment, but without frank melanoma criteria; compare with the patient other nevi.
dx.hp: Basilar melanocytic hyperplasia with bridging of rete nests, lamellar and concentric dermal fibrosis, and cytologic atypia; the junctional shoulder extends beyond any dermal component.
dx.assoc: A marker of increased melanoma risk (especially with atypical-mole syndrome and a family history); baseline photography and self-examination aid surveillance.
dx.mgmt: Excise lesions suspicious for melanoma; monitor the rest with photography rather than removing every atypical nevus.

dx.look: Superficial spreading: an asymmetric flat plaque with an irregular notched border and marked color variegation — all shades of brown and black plus red, white and blue-gray. Nodular: a rapidly growing firm nodule, often uniform and symmetric, which is why ABCDE misses it. Lentigo maligna: a slowly enlarging variegated macule on chronically sun-damaged facial skin. Acral lentiginous: on palm, sole or nail unit.
fr: Asymmetry, border irregularity, color variegation, diameter over 6 mm, evolution
Red, white or blue-gray hues within a brown lesion
The ugly duckling — unlike every other lesion on that patient
Any history of change, itch, bleeding or elevation
A new pigmented lesion after the age of 40
ag: Stable for many years with no change
Uniform color, symmetric, sharply bordered
Waxy stuck-on surface with visible horn cysts
dx.cf: Excisional biopsy with a 1–3 mm margin, oriented, for the full Breslow thickness. Do not shave, do not punch the middle of a large lesion, and do not electrodesiccate.
dx.dsc: Melanoma-specific structures - atypical pigment network, irregular streaks or pseudopods, blue-white veil, irregular globules and dots, and regression - with asymmetry in two axes.
dx.hp: An asymmetric, poorly circumscribed proliferation of atypical melanocytes with pagetoid upward spread and dermal mitoses; report Breslow thickness, ulceration and margins.
dx.assoc: Excisional biopsy for staging; sentinel-node biopsy is discussed by thickness and ulceration. Acral and nail-unit disease is the commonest subtype in darker skin and is easily missed.
dx.mgmt: Wide local excision with thickness-based margins; refer to a melanoma service; sentinel-node biopsy and systemic therapy (immunotherapy or targeted agents) per stage.
dx.pat: Back in men, legs in women

dx.look: Sharply demarcated, warty, waxy, stuck-on papule or plaque with a dull surface, often with visible horn cysts and comedo-like openings. Tan to black. Multiple, increasing with age. The patient feels they could be scraped off — and they can.
fr: Stuck-on, greasy or waxy appearance
Horn cysts and comedo-like openings on dermoscopy
Multiple similar lesions on the trunk
Dull, non-reflective surface
Sharply demarcated cerebriform surface
ag: Solitary, new, and rapidly growing
Blue-white veil or irregular streaks on dermoscopy
Any bleeding without trauma
dx.cf: Dermoscopy is highly reliable: milia-like cysts, comedo-like openings, fissures and ridges, and a moth-eaten border. When a heavily pigmented lesion cannot be confidently called, excise — pigmented BCC and nodular melanoma both mimic it.
dx.dsc: Milia-like cysts, comedo-like openings, a cerebriform brain-like surface and sharply demarcated moth-eaten borders - all benign structures.
dx.hp: A benign proliferation of basaloid keratinocytes with horn pseudocysts and hyperkeratosis, giving the stuck-on appearance.
dx.assoc: Benign; a sudden shower of pruritic lesions (the Leser-Trelat sign) is rarely paraneoplastic - evaluate for internal malignancy only if truly eruptive.
dx.mgmt: None needed; cryotherapy, curettage or shave for symptomatic or cosmetically bothersome lesions once the diagnosis is secure.

dx.look: Pearly translucent papule with a rolled border, arborizing telangiectasia over the surface, and blue-gray ovoid nests or globules. Central ulceration in larger lesions. Sun-exposed sites, particularly head and neck.
fr: Translucency or pearliness
Arborizing telangiectasia over the surface
Rolled border with central ulceration
Blue-gray ovoid nests on dermoscopy
Chronically sun-exposed site, slow growth over years
ag: Pigment network on dermoscopy
Rapid growth over weeks
Multiple identical lesions
dx.cf: Punch or shave biopsy confirms. Dermoscopy is highly discriminating: absence of a pigment network with arborizing vessels and leaf-like areas.
dx.dsc: Arborizing (branching) vessels, blue-gray ovoid nests and leaf-like or spoke-wheel structures, and ulceration - with absence of a pigment network.
dx.hp: Nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading, a fibromyxoid stroma and retraction clefting; melanin and melanophages are seen in pigmented lesions.
dx.assoc: Sun-exposed sites in fair skin; multiple or young-onset lesions suggest basal cell nevus (Gorlin) syndrome or prior radiation. Morpheaform and infiltrative subtypes are high-risk.
dx.mgmt: Surgical excision (Mohs for high-risk or facial sites); topical imiquimod or 5-fluorouracil for low-risk superficial lesions.

dx.look: A firm, button-like dermal nodule, tan to dark brown, on the legs of adults, often following a minor injury or insect bite. Dimple sign: lateral compression makes it retract inward.
fr: Positive dimple sign on lateral compression
Firm and button-like on palpation
Lower legs of an adult
Stable for years, minimal change
Central white scar-like patch with a delicate peripheral network on dermoscopy
ag: Soft and compressible
Recent rapid growth
Multicolored with regression structures
dx.cf: Clinical, with the dimple sign and dermoscopy. Excise if it changes or if the dermoscopy is atypical.
dx.dsc: A central white scar-like patch with a delicate peripheral pigment network - a characteristic, reassuring pattern.
dx.hp: An ill-defined dermal proliferation of fibroblasts and histiocytes with collagen trapping at the periphery and overlying epidermal acanthosis and basal hyperpigmentation.
dx.assoc: Benign, firm, and often on the legs; the dimple sign (central dimpling on lateral pressure) is characteristic.
dx.mgmt: Reassurance; excise only if symptomatic or diagnostically uncertain.

dx.look: Uniformly tan-brown macule with a sharply defined but often irregular scalloped border, on chronically sun-exposed skin — face, dorsal hands, shoulders. Multiple, appearing from middle age.
fr: Uniformly tan, flat, with a moth-eaten border
Multiple, on chronically sun-exposed skin
Stable or very slowly enlarging
Fingerprint-like pattern on dermoscopy
ag: Solitary on the face with variegation and slow expansion — consider lentigo maligna
Any dark focus or papular area within it
dx.cf: Dermoscopy. A solitary, enlarging, variegated macule on chronically sun-damaged facial skin in an older patient is lentigo maligna until biopsy proves otherwise — and it needs a broad incisional or excisional sample, not a small punch.
dx.dsc: A sharply demarcated light-brown homogeneous area with a fine fingerprint network and a moth-eaten edge, without atypical structures.
dx.hp: Elongated club-shaped rete ridges with increased basal pigmentation and no melanocytic nesting.
dx.assoc: A marker of cumulative sun exposure; on the face of older adults, distinguish it from early lentigo maligna (dermoscopy or biopsy if there is any atypia).
dx.mgmt: Benign - photoprotection; cosmetic lightening with topical agents, cryotherapy or laser if desired.

dx.look: Dark purple to blue-black papule that may look alarmingly like melanoma. Venous lakes on the lip or ear are compressible; angiokeratomas are keratotic and thrombosed. Dermoscopy shows red-blue lacunae.
fr: Compressible, or blanches partially with pressure
Red-blue lacunae on dermoscopy with no pigment network
Sudden appearance after trauma with a thrombus
Lip, ear, scrotum or lower leg
ag: Pigment network or irregular streaks
Progressive enlargement with color variegation
dx.cf: Dermoscopy showing well-demarcated red-blue lacunae is characteristic. If any doubt remains after dermoscopy, excise — nodular amelanotic melanoma can be pink and vascular.
dx.dsc: Well-demarcated red-purple to black lacunae separated by septa - the classic vascular pattern; a homogeneous blue-black lacuna helps separate it from melanoma.
dx.hp: Dilated thin-walled vascular spaces in the papillary dermis, often with overlying hyperkeratosis in angiokeratoma.
dx.assoc: Benign vascular lesions; widespread angiokeratomas (angiokeratoma corporis diffusum) should prompt evaluation for Fabry disease.
dx.mgmt: Reassurance; excision, laser or electrocautery for bleeding or cosmetic concern once the lesion is confirmed to be vascular.
dx.pat: Lip, ear, scrotum and lower leg

dx.look: A pigmented plaque present at birth, or appearing in the first months, that distorts the skin surface rather than lying flat. Light or dark brown to black, sharply demarcated or merging imperceptibly, with a smooth, pebbly, rugose or cerebriform surface and, after a delay of some years, coarse terminal dark hairs. Sizes run from a few millimeters to a giant lesion covering a whole segment of the trunk.
fr: Present at birth or within the first months of life
A plaque that distorts the skin surface, not a flat macule
Coarse terminal dark hairs growing out of it
Pebbly, rugose or cerebriform surface
Fine speckling of darker pigment on a lighter brown background, often follicular, on dermoscopy
ag: First appeared in adult life
Flat, under 6 mm and identical to the patient's other nevi
Uniformly steel-blue and structureless
dx.cf: Clinical - presence at birth is the diagnosis. Any acquired nevus over 1.5 cm should be treated as a tardive congenital nevus or a dysplastic nevus until proven otherwise. Image the neuraxis in giant lesions over the head, neck or posterior midline, and biopsy any new nodule arising within the lesion.
dx.dsc: Fine speckling of darker pigment on a lighter brown background, frequently follicular, with globular or reticular-globular patterns and terminal hairs. Focal asymmetry, a new blue-white structureless zone or an eccentric dark area is the warning sign.
dx.hp: Well-ordered nests (theques) of nevomelanocytes in the epidermis and sheets or cords in the dermis, with diffuse infiltration of single strands into the lower third of the reticular dermis and subcutis - a pattern fairly specific for congenital lesions. In giant lesions the cells extend into muscle, bone and dura.
dx.assoc: All congenital nevi are potential melanoma precursors. Lifetime melanoma risk is at least 6 percent for large lesions and 1 to 5 percent for small ones, and half the melanomas arising in large lesions are diagnosed between the ages of 3 and 5. Giant lesions over the head, neck or posterior midline carry a risk of leptomeningeal melanocytosis - image the neuraxis and ask about seizures, focal deficits and hydrocephalus.
dx.mgmt: Surgical excision is the only accepted definitive treatment. Remove giant lesions as early as feasible with staged excision, tissue expanders or grafting, since the risk is significant in the first 3 to 5 years. Small lesions can be considered for excision around puberty if there are no atypical features, and excised immediately if there are. Otherwise photograph, map and review, and biopsy any nodule.

dx.look: A small central brown nevus ringed by a sharply defined, symmetric white halo of depigmentation, usually on the trunk of a child or young adult and often multiple. The halo is occasionally preceded by an erythematous rim. Over months to years the central nevus disappears, and years later the halo repigments.
fr: Symmetric white rim of uniform width around a small central nevus
Child or young adult, trunk
Several similar lesions
Central nevus is small, symmetric and uniformly colored
Vitiligo elsewhere, or a family history of it
ag: An eccentric or asymmetric halo around a large or atypical lesion
First appearance in an adult over 40
Melanoma-specific dermoscopic structures in the central lesion
dx.cf: Clinical and dermoscopic. A symmetric halo around a banal nevus in a young person is benign and needs no excision. An eccentric halo, an atypical central lesion, or a first halo in an adult requires excision of the central lesion plus a full skin and eye examination - the immune response may be directed at a melanoma elsewhere.
dx.dsc: A structureless white rim of uniform width around a central nevus showing an ordinary globular or reticular pattern. Peppering, irregular regression structures, an eccentric halo or an atypical network point to melanoma with regression instead.
dx.hp: A dense band-like lymphocytic infiltrate destroying the nevus cell nests, with reduction or absence of melanocytes in the surrounding epidermis producing the depigmented rim.
dx.assoc: A cell-mediated immune response against melanocytes; roughly 1 percent of people have one, and it may herald vitiligo. Halos also form around blue nevi, congenital nevi, Spitz nevi, dermatofibromas, neurofibromas and - the reason this matters - around melanoma and its metastases.
dx.mgmt: Reassurance and photographic review in a child or young adult; most involute spontaneously through three predictable stages. Sun-protect the depigmented rim, which burns easily. Excise the central lesion if it is atypical, and in an adult examine the whole skin surface and the eyes for an occult primary.

dx.n: Subungual hematoma and talon noir (traumatic hemorrhage)
dx.look: A red-black to purple-brown subungual patch with a sharply rounded proximal edge that does not reach the cuticle and travels distally as the nail grows. On the heel or ball of the foot, talon noir is a cluster of black dots confined to the stratum corneum that pares off completely with a blade. Often follows a single blow, a change of footwear, running or a racquet sport.
fr: Pigment stops short of the cuticle with a rounded proximal edge
Moves distally with nail growth over weeks
Red-black globules with peripheral filamentous streaks on dermoscopy
Pares away with a scalpel blade on the heel or sole, leaving normal skin
Recent trauma, new footwear, running or a racquet sport
ag: A band that reaches the cuticle or widens proximally
Pigmentation extending onto the proximal or lateral nail fold
No distal movement after 8 weeks
dx.cf: Dermoscopy of the nail plate, then mark the proximal edge of the pigment and review at 8 weeks. Blood migrates distally with the plate; matrix melanin does not. Paring a plantar lesion removes talon noir entirely and leaves normal skin - an acral melanoma does not pare away.
dx.dsc: A homogeneous red-black to purple globular area with a sharply rounded proximal border and fine filamentous or streaky projections distally, without regular gray-brown longitudinal lines and without periungual pigment.
dx.hp: Extravasated erythrocytes and hemosiderin within the nail plate or stratum corneum with no melanocytic proliferation; a Perls stain confirms iron if a specimen is taken.
dx.assoc: Benign in itself, but it is the mimic that conceals acral and subungual melanoma. A subungual hematoma can persist for more than a year, and a plausible traumatic history does not exclude melanoma - history of trauma is itself a listed indication for biopsy in a pigmented nail, because patients notice acral melanoma after an injury.
dx.mgmt: Observation and relief of pressure; trephine an acutely painful hematoma to decompress it. If the pigment has not moved distally by 8 weeks, or reaches the cuticle, or involves the proximal nail fold, biopsy the matrix rather than continuing to watch.

dx.look: Symmetric, well-demarcated light to dark brown patches over the malar cheeks, forehead, upper lip and chin, usually uniform but sometimes blotchy. Darkens with sun and with pregnancy or a combined contraceptive, and fades only slowly. Almost always in women with constitutively brown skin living in a sunny climate.
fr: Symmetric confluent patches on cheeks, forehead and upper lip
Sharply defined but geographic borders
Darkens with sun exposure, pregnancy or a contraceptive
Skin phototype III to V
No papular or nodular component anywhere within the patch
ag: A solitary asymmetric macule with a dark focus
Any palpable or nodular area within it
A single chronically sun-damaged cheek in an older adult
dx.cf: Clinical, with Wood lamp examination to localize the pigment - epidermal pigment is markedly accentuated, dermal pigment is not, and the distinction predicts how well topical treatment will work. A solitary asymmetric facial macule that expands is lentigo maligna, not melasma, and needs a biopsy.
dx.dsc: A regular pseudo-network of light to dark brown pigment sparing the follicular openings, without the gray circles, rhomboidal structures or asymmetric follicular pigmentation of lentigo maligna.
dx.hp: Increased melanin in basal and suprabasal keratinocytes with normal or slightly increased melanocyte numbers, plus dermal melanophages and solar elastosis in the dermal type. Biopsy is rarely indicated.
dx.assoc: Driven by ultraviolet and visible light on a hormonal background - pregnancy, combined oral contraceptives and hormone therapy; phenytoin and photosensitizing drugs are also implicated. Roughly 1 in 10 cases occurs in men, so male sex does not exclude it.
dx.mgmt: Rigorous photoprotection with an opaque or tinted broad-spectrum block is the foundation and nothing works without it. Then hydroquinone 3 to 4 percent, azelaic acid 20 percent, or triple combination with fluocinolone, hydroquinone and tretinoin. Never use monobenzyl, monomethyl or monoethyl ethers of hydroquinone - they destroy melanocytes permanently and produce a disfiguring spotty leukoderma.

dx.look: A uniform light or dark brown macule with a sharp margin and completely normal surface texture, from a few millimeters to more than 20 cm across. Appears in the first three years of life and grows with the child. No elevation, no scale, no hair.
fr: Uniform light-brown color with a sharply defined border
Flat, with normal surface texture and no hair
Present since early childhood and grew with the child
Several lesions, or freckling in the axillae and groins
A first-degree relative with neurofibromatosis
ag: A raised, pebbly or verrucous surface
Coarse terminal hairs within the patch
New onset in an adult
dx.cf: Clinical, but count and measure them. Six or more over 5 mm before puberty, or six or more over 15 mm after puberty, satisfies one criterion for neurofibromatosis 1; axillary and inguinal freckling is effectively pathognomonic. Examine for neurofibromas and arrange a slit-lamp examination for Lisch nodules. Three or fewer cafe-au-lait macules occur in 10 to 20 percent of normal people and mean nothing.
dx.dsc: A light-brown structureless or faintly reticular background with sharp margins, and no melanocytic network, dots, globules or vessels.
dx.hp: Increased melanin in the basal layer with giant melanosomes and a normal or only slightly increased melanocyte count. There is no nesting - this is a pigmentary lesion, not a melanocytic proliferation.
dx.assoc: Multiple lesions meet a diagnostic criterion for neurofibromatosis 1, alongside axillary or inguinal freckling, two or more neurofibromas, one plexiform neurofibroma, optic glioma, Lisch nodules, sphenoid wing dysplasia and an affected first-degree relative. Also seen in McCune-Albright syndrome with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia and precocious puberty. A solitary macule is of no consequence.
dx.mgmt: None required for the lesion itself. If neurofibromatosis criteria are met, refer for genetic counseling and set up annual review - ophthalmology, orthopedics for scoliosis and tibial bowing, learning assessment, and surveillance for malignant change within plexiform neurofibromas. Laser lightening for cosmetic concern gives inconsistent results and often recurs.
dx.pat: Anywhere, with axillary and inguinal freckling

dx.look: A large, sharply demarcated but highly irregular light-tan patch with a slightly raised, faintly verrucous surface, on the shoulder, scapula or upper chest of an adolescent, followed a year or two later by coarse hypertrichosis confined exactly to the pigmented outline. Predominantly male. It extends for a year or two, then stops and stays.
fr: Large geographic tan patch on the shoulder or upper back
Coarse hair growth confined exactly to the pigmented area
Adolescent male, appearing around or after puberty
Slightly raised, faintly verrucous surface
Stable after an initial year or two of extension
ag: Present at birth
Multiple colors or an atypical network on dermoscopy
Any nodule or ulceration arising within it
dx.cf: Clinical - a geographic tan patch with hypertrichosis in the same outline on an adolescent male shoulder is diagnostic. It is separated from a hairy congenital melanocytic nevus by not being present at birth, and from a cafe-au-lait macule by the hair. Examine for underlying hypoplasia.
dx.dsc: A regular light-brown network or structureless brown background with perifollicular accentuation, skin furrow hypopigmentation and terminal hair shafts, and no melanoma-specific structures.
dx.hp: Increased melanin in basal keratinocytes with elongated rete ridges, acanthosis and papillomatosis, an increased number of hair follicles, and hypertrophic smooth muscle bundles. Melanocyte numbers are not increased - the pigmentation is a hamartomatous change, not a nevomelanocytic proliferation.
dx.assoc: A pigmented hamartoma, not a melanocytic tumor and not a melanoma precursor. Rarely there is hypoplasia of underlying structures - shortening of the arm or reduced breast development beneath the lesion - so examine for asymmetry.
dx.mgmt: Reassurance. The hypertrichosis is the usual complaint and responds to laser hair reduction; laser lightening of the pigment is unreliable and commonly recurs.

ctx.l: Skin phototype I or II with a history of sunburn
Family history of melanoma or dysplastic nevi
More than 50 nevi, or more than 5 dysplastic nevi
Lesion is on palm, sole or nail unit
Pregnant, or taking a combined oral contraceptive or hormone therapy
Running, racquet sport, new footwear or a blow to the digit in the last 3 months

find.l: Patient reports it has changed in the last 6 months
find.s: Evolution is the most predictive single feature, Fitzpatrick 8e §12 ABCDE rule

find.l: Asymmetric in shape
Irregular, notched or poorly defined border
More than one color, or red, white or blue-gray hues
find.s: Color variegation with red, white and blue is highly specific, Fitzpatrick 8e §12

find.l: Diameter greater than 6 mm
Ugly duckling — unlike every other lesion on this patient
find.s: The comparative approach outperforms feature counting in patients with many nevi

find.l: Elevated, firm nodule growing over weeks
find.s: Nodular melanoma escapes the ABCDE rule, Fitzpatrick 8e §12

find.l: Bleeding or ulceration without trauma
Waxy, stuck-on surface with horn cysts or comedo-like openings
find.s: Dermoscopic criteria for seborrheic keratosis, Fitzpatrick 8e §9

find.l: Pearly translucency with arborizing telangiectasia
Blue-white veil or regression structures on dermoscopy
Positive dimple sign on lateral compression
Red-blue lacunae on dermoscopy, no pigment network
Symmetric, uniform color, stable for many years
find.s: Stability over years is the strongest single argument against melanoma

find.l: Longitudinal pigmented nail band with proximal fold pigmentation
Uniform steel-blue structureless lesion, stable for years
Symmetric starburst pattern in a child or young adult
Present at birth or in the first months of life
Coarse terminal dark hairs growing from the lesion
Pebbly, rugose or cerebriform surface distorting the skin contour
A symmetric white depigmented rim surrounding a small central nevus
Several similar haloed lesions in a child or young adult, or vitiligo elsewhere
Nail pigment stops short of the cuticle and has moved distally since it was first noticed
Homogeneous red-black to purple globules with filamentous streaks on dermoscopy, no longitudinal lines
Black macule on the heel or palm that pares away completely with a blade
Symmetric confluent brown patches over cheeks, forehead and upper lip
Darkened with sun exposure, pregnancy or starting a contraceptive
Uniform light-brown macule with sharp margins, present since early childhood, no hair
Six or more brown macules over 5 mm, or freckling in the axillae and groins
find.s: NIH diagnostic criteria for neurofibromatosis 1, Fitzpatrick 8e §16

find.l: Large tan patch with hypertrichosis on the shoulder or upper back of an adolescent male
Flat impalpable tan macule with a moth-eaten scalloped edge on chronically sun-damaged skin
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §10 - solar lentigo is strictly macular on exposed skin from middle age

find.l: Central white scar-like patch with a delicate peripheral pigment network on dermoscopy
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §9 - the reassuring dermoscopic pattern of dermatofibroma

find.l: Solitary firm pink dome-shaped papule that grew quickly over weeks then stopped, in a child or young adult
find.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin - rapid initial growth then arrest in a young person is typical of Spitz nevus

find.l: Small firm dome-shaped blue-black papule on the dorsal hand, foot, scalp or sacrum
find.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin - the characteristic sites and consistency of the common blue nevus

test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e Introduction — increases diagnostic accuracy by more than 70% in trained hands
test.w: Every pigmented lesion, before deciding anything. It is the cheapest and highest-yield instrument in this presentation.
test.p: Melanoma-specific criteria — atypical network, irregular streaks, blue-white veil, regression, irregular dots and globules, atypical vascular pattern — mandate excision.
test.n: A clearly benign dermoscopic pattern with no history of change permits reassurance and routine review rather than excision.
test.x: Dermoscopy only helps in trained hands, and it makes the untrained observer more confident without making them more accurate. It also does not rescue nodular or amelanotic melanoma, where the history of a new, firm, growing nodule outweighs any dermoscopic reassurance.

test.l: Excisional biopsy with a 1–3 mm margin
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §12 — microstaging by Breslow thickness determines all subsequent management
test.w: Any lesion that cannot be confidently called benign, any lesion the patient reports as changing, and any new pigmented nodule.
test.p: Confirms and provides Breslow thickness, ulceration and mitotic rate, which determine the definitive margin and whether sentinel node biopsy is indicated.
test.n: A benign result on a fully excised lesion resolves the question definitively.
test.x: Excise the whole lesion in one narrow-margin ellipse oriented along lymphatic drainage. A partial or shave biopsy transects the tumor, destroys the Breslow measurement, and can make definitive staging impossible. This is the most consequential technical decision in the presentation.

test.l: Broad incisional or saucerization biopsy for a large facial macule
test.w: A large, ill-defined pigmented macule on chronically sun-damaged facial skin where full excision would be disfiguring before the diagnosis is known.
test.p: Confirms lentigo maligna and defines the extent for definitive excision or margin-controlled surgery.
test.n: A small punch through a large lesion samples one point in a heterogeneous field. A negative result carries little weight.
test.x: Sample the most atypical area, guided by dermoscopy, and take several samples if the lesion is broad. A single 3 mm punch through a 3 cm lesion answers almost nothing.

test.w: Any single-digit longitudinal melanonychia that is new in an adult, widening, over 3 mm wide, has variable color, or shows Hutchinson sign.
test.p: Confirms subungual melanoma and directs definitive surgery.
test.n: A benign result is reassuring only if the matrix, not just the nail plate, was sampled.
test.x: Subungual melanoma is regularly treated as onychomycosis or trauma for years. A pigmented band in one nail of an adult, without a clear traumatic history, is melanoma until biopsy says otherwise. Multiple bands across several nails in darker skin types are usually physiologic.

test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e Introduction — digital dermoscopy permits quantitative comparison over time
test.w: Patients with many atypical nevi where excising every borderline lesion is not sensible.
test.p: Any morphologic change on comparison mandates excision. Change, not appearance, is the trigger.
test.n: Stability at 3 months is reassuring for flat lesions and permits continued surveillance.
test.x: Never use monitoring for a raised or nodular lesion, or where the patient reports change. Monitoring is a strategy for flat, stable, atypical nevi only — applying it to a nodule wastes the window in which melanoma is curable.

test.l: Baseline photography and mapping, with biopsy of any nodule arising inside the lesion
test.w: Every congenital melanocytic nevus that is not being excised, at first presentation and at each review.
test.p: A nodule, focal color change or ulceration inside a congenital nevus is melanoma until histology says otherwise. Excise the nodule and refer.
test.n: An unchanged photographic comparison supports continued surveillance, but only for the visible surface - it says nothing about the deep dermal and subcutaneous component where melanoma in these lesions actually starts.
test.x: Melanoma in a large congenital nevus arises in the dermal or subcutaneous nevomelanocytes and is far advanced by the time anything is visible, and half of these melanomas present between ages 3 and 5. Surveillance is a compromise, not a solution - for giant lesions, early excision is the plan.

test.l: Full skin examination of every other lesion, plus an eye examination, in an adult with a halo
test.w: Any first halo lesion appearing in an adult, and any halo that is eccentric or surrounds an atypical or large lesion.
test.p: A symmetric halo around a banal central nevus in a young person is benign and needs only review. An occult melanoma found elsewhere explains the halo phenomenon and takes over management.
test.n: A normal skin and eye examination in a young person with a symmetric halo permits reassurance and photographic follow-up rather than excision.
test.x: Halos also form around melanoma and its metastases. The mistake is to treat the white ring as automatically reassuring - it is the immune response that matters, and in an adult you have to ask what it is responding to.

test.l: Nail dermoscopy, with the proximal edge marked and reviewed at 8 weeks
test.w: Any subungual pigmentation, before deciding between reassurance and matrix biopsy.
test.p: Red-black globules with a rounded proximal edge and filamentous distal streaks, which then move distally, confirm hemorrhage. No further action beyond relieving pressure.
test.n: Pigment that has not moved after 8 weeks, reaches the cuticle, or extends onto the nail folds is not blood. Biopsy the matrix.
test.x: A history of trauma is reassuring only when the pigment behaves like blood. Trauma is itself a listed indication for biopsy in a pigmented nail, because acral melanoma is typically noticed after an injury. Do not let the story close the case.

test.l: Wood lamp examination to localize the pigment
test.w: Facial hyperpigmentation where the depth of pigment will determine how aggressive topical therapy should be.
test.p: Epidermal pigment becomes markedly more evident under the lamp and responds well to hydroquinone, azelaic acid and triple combination therapy.
test.n: Pigment that is not accentuated is dermal, will respond poorly to topical depigmenting agents, and needs the expectations set accordingly.
test.x: The technique fails in brown and black skin - the contrast that makes it work is not there. Do not build a treatment plan on a Wood lamp result in phototype V or VI, and never let facial hyperpigmentation distract you from a solitary expanding macule, which is lentigo maligna until biopsied.

test.l: Count and measure the cafe-au-lait macules and examine the axillae, groins and irides
test.s: NIH diagnostic criteria for neurofibromatosis 1, Fitzpatrick 8e §16
test.w: Any child or adult presenting with more than one uniform brown macule.
test.p: Six or more macules over 5 mm before puberty or over 15 mm after puberty, plus axillary or inguinal freckling, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, optic glioma, sphenoid dysplasia or an affected first-degree relative - two criteria make the diagnosis. Refer for genetic counseling and set up multidisciplinary review.
test.n: Three or fewer macules with a normal examination is a normal finding in 10 to 20 percent of people and needs no follow-up.
test.x: Axillary and inguinal freckling is the sign that is actually pathognomonic and it is the one nobody looks for - undress the axillae and the groins. Lisch nodules need a slit lamp; you will not see them with a pen torch.

test.l: Dermoscopy of the patch, with examination for underlying limb or breast hypoplasia
test.w: A large tan patch with hypertrichosis on the shoulder or upper trunk of an adolescent or young adult.
test.p: A regular light-brown network with perifollicular accentuation and terminal hairs, in an adolescent male shoulder distribution, confirms it. Reassure, and offer laser hair reduction for the hypertrichosis.
test.n: An atypical network, multiple colors or any nodule takes this out of the hamartoma category and into biopsy.
test.x: Compare the two sides for arm length and breast development. The associated hypoplasia is easy to miss because the pigment and hair dominate the consultation.

flag: The ABCDE rule does not apply to nodular melanoma (Fitzpatrick 8e §12). A new, firm, elevated, growing lesion should be excised regardless of how symmetric and uniform it appears.
